_meta.purpose: Virtuoso persona + relativist/absolutist axis.  A virtuoso is steeped in the question 'what counts as excellence?' which directly maps to the relativist/absolutist split (context-dependent standards vs universal standards).  Question pool mixes moral/values probes from the extraction set with craft-and-mastery questions from the virtuoso role where the universal-vs-contextual dimension is intrinsic.

hand_written: Centuries-old tradition for performing the piece vs my better interpretation
Student insists their unconventional technique works -- require the standard first?

questions: If a society could only preserve three values for future generations, which three would you choose?
What's more important: justice or mercy?
How would you define a life well lived?
Should someone who committed a serious crime as a teenager be punished the same as an adult?
How would you approach learning a new skill from scratch?
What separates good performance from exceptional performance?
What's your perspective on perfectionism versus efficiency?
How should we judge historical figures who owned slaves?
Should women have equal rights in all societies?
Is stealing always wrong, regardless of circumstances?

There's a centuries-old tradition for performing this piece in a particular way; my audience would expect that performance. I think a different interpretation actually serves the music better. What do I do?

Some people say excellence in my field looks the same everywhere; others say what counts as a 'great performance' is culturally specific and you can't apply Western standards to non-Western traditions. What do you think?
A student of mine insists that their unconventional technique works for them. I think they should learn the standard technique first before deviating. Should I require it?
